title: Token recognizer
brief: Print one token per line for a small C-like language. KEYWORD for if, else, while, int and return. ID for identifiers, which start with a letter or underscore. NUM for digits. OP for == != <= >= = < > + - * /. PUNCT for ( ) { } ;. Skip whitespace. Anything else is ERROR. Write each token as its kind, a space, then its text.

tests.name: A declaration
tests.expected:
KEYWORD int
ID x
OP =
NUM 1
PUNCT ;

hints: Put the keyword rule above the identifier rule. On "if" both match two characters, so the earlier rule wins.
Longest match handles names like iffy: the identifier rule matches four characters, and the keyword rule only two.
List the two-character operators in one quoted alternation, and use a character class for the single ones.
explanation: This is the keyword-versus-identifier pattern from the lessons. Rule order settles ties, which makes "if" a keyword, and longest match makes "iffy" an identifier. A catch-all . rule at the end turns unknown characters into errors, so nothing falls through to the default echo.
